strengths: Addresses a genuinely underexplored problem: no prior TTA method exists for vision-language object detectors (VLODs), and the paper carefully motivates why classification-style TTA (entropy minimization, prompt averaging) transfers poorly to detection due to confirmation bias and lack of proposal-structure awareness.

The two proposed components (IoU-weighted entropy minimization and image-conditioned prompt selection) are simple, lightweight, and well-motivated with clear illustrative examples (Figs. 1-2) showing concrete failure modes they address.

Extensive empirical evaluation: 6+ datasets/benchmarks (stylized domains, driving scenes, low-light, PASCAL-C, COCO-C), 15 corruption types across 5 severities, two architecturally different detectors (CNN-based YOLO-World and transformer-based Grounding DINO), and multiple backbone sizes (YW-L, GD-B), totaling many test scenarios.

Thorough ablation studies covering IoU threshold, cluster exponent, fusion coefficient, prompt-selection fraction, adapter placement per module, batch size, augmentation count, and prompt-generation strategy, which supports reproducibility and gives insight into the mechanism of the method.
Reasonable baselines adapted from VLM TTA literature (TPT, VPT, DPE) and a fair Adapter+TENT baseline, allowing isolation of the contribution of IWE/IPS beyond simply using adapters.
Additional analyses such as computational overhead/FPS comparison, effect of pre-adaptation fine-tuning, and qualitative visualizations strengthen the completeness of the empirical study.
A simple theoretical remark (cosine-Euclidean equivalence) is included, and the paper is generally clearly written with a coherent narrative connecting motivation, method, and results.
weaknesses: Gains are inconsistent and sometimes marginal in challenging domains (e.g., driving scenes with small, low-overlap objects), and the paper's own conclusion admits IWE underperforms in such settings, which somewhat limits the claimed generality of the method.

On COCO-C (Tables 8-10), standard entropy-based Adapter/TENT baseline occasionally outperforms VLOD-TTA on specific corruptions, indicating the proposed IWE objective does not uniformly dominate simpler baselines, particularly for the harder 80-class setting.

Adapter placement differs per detector (vision/neck adapters for YW vs. text-encoder-only for GD), determined empirically through ablation on the same style-shift datasets used for the main benchmark; this raises a mild concern about hyperparameter/architecture-choice overfitting to the evaluation suite rather than a principled a priori design choice.

The prompt pool used for IPS is generated by GPT without dataset-specific information, but its quality/diversity is not controlled for or compared against a wider variety of automatically generated pools; the reported gains from IPS could be sensitive to the particular prompt set chosen (dataset-specific prompts give notably larger gains, suggesting some sensitivity).

The method requires single-step gradient adaptation per image (backward pass), and although FPS is reported, the throughput drop relative to ZS (89→20 FPS on YW) is substantial, which may limit applicability in real-time detection settings central to the motivating driving/AR use cases.

Comparisons are restricted to VLM-style TTA baselines adapted to detection; no comparison is made to detection-native TTA methods (e.g., Chen et al. 2023, Yoo et al. 2023, Cao et al. 2025) discussed in related work, even though these are specifically designed for object detectors, leaving open whether VLOD-TTA's advantage stems mainly from being detection-aware versus VLM-style baselines being poorly suited by design.
No code/artifact link is provided in the submission (placeholder only), which affects immediate reproducibility despite detailed hyperparameter reporting in the appendix.

strengths: Addresses a clearly identified gap: no prior TTA method exists specifically for vision-language object detectors (VLODs), and the paper is positioned as the first such framework.

The two proposed components (IoU-weighted entropy minimization and image-conditioned prompt selection) are well-motivated with clear qualitative illustrations (Figs. 1-2) showing the specific failure modes of standard entropy minimization and prompt averaging in the detection setting.

Extensive empirical evaluation spanning style shift, driving scenes, low-light, and 15 common corruptions across two architecturally distinct VLODs (CNN-based YOLO-World and transformer-based Grounding DINO), totaling many test scenarios, with consistent (if sometimes modest) improvements over zero-shot and adapted classification-style TTA baselines.

Thorough ablation studies covering adapter placement per module, prompt generation strategy, batch size, augmentation count, backbone scale, IoU threshold/cluster exponent/fusion coefficient/selection fraction sensitivity, and the effect of pre-adaptation fine-tuning, which supports reproducibility and provides practical guidance.
Computational overhead (FPS, trainable parameters) is reported and compared against baselines, showing a favorable robustness-cost trade-off relative to other adapted TTA methods.
Honest discussion of limitations (e.g., IWE underperforming on scenes with many small, low-overlap objects such as Cityscapes) rather than overselling uniform gains.
weaknesses: The method relies on several sensitive hyperparameters (IoU threshold θ, cluster exponent γ, top-M proposals, prompt selection fraction ρ, fusion coefficient λ) that are tuned differently per detector architecture (e.g., different λ for YW vs GD, different adapter placement per model); this undermines the practicality of a genuine label-free test-time adaptation setting, since such tuning implicitly requires access to target-domain validation performance.

No empirical comparison to existing TTA-for-object-detection methods (e.g., Chen et al. 2023, Yoo et al. 2023, Cao et al. 2025, Ruan & Tang 2024) that are discussed in related work but not benchmarked, even though they could plausibly be adapted to VLODs similarly to the VLM baselines; this leaves open whether the gains are specific to the VLOD setting or achievable by existing detection-TTA ideas.

Reported gains are modest in several important scenarios (e.g., ~1 mAP/AP50 average improvement on Cityscapes/BDD100K driving scenes), and the paper itself notes several corruptions in COCO-C where standard entropy/Adapter baselines match or exceed VLOD-TTA, somewhat diluting the strength of the central claims.

The IoU-based clustering weight relies on the detector's own (potentially noisy) predicted class label (argmax) to form class-specific graphs, creating a bootstrapping dependency on proposal quality that is not analyzed theoretically or stress-tested under severe class-confusion conditions.
No variance/statistical significance reporting across runs (single-seed numbers throughout), which is a concern for a method with stochastic single-step adaptation per image.

The core technical novelty is relatively incremental: both components are heuristic reweightings/selections layered on well-established entropy minimization and prompt-ensembling ideas rather than fundamentally new mechanisms, which may limit the broader scientific contribution despite solid engineering and benchmarking effort.

strengths: Addresses a clearly identified gap: no prior TTA method exists for vision-language object detectors, and the paper is explicit that adapting classification-oriented TTA (entropy minimization, prompt tuning, cache-based methods) to detection is non-trivial due to the presence of many proposals coupled with localization.

The two proposed components (IoU-weighted entropy minimization and image-conditioned prompt selection) are well motivated with clear illustrative failure cases (Figs. 1-2) showing why naive entropy minimization and prompt averaging fail for VLODs.

Extensive empirical evaluation: 6 mainstream detection datasets plus PASCAL-C/COCO-C with 15 corruption types across 5 severities, on two structurally different VLODs (CNN-based YOLO-World and transformer-based Grounding DINO), totaling many distinct test scenarios.

Strong set of adapted baselines (TPT, VPT, DPE, Adapter/TENT) gives a fair comparison point since no existing VLOD-specific TTA baseline exists, and the method consistently outperforms them across nearly all settings.

Thorough ablation studies covering IoU threshold, cluster exponent, fusion coefficient, number of selected prompts, adapter placement per module, batch size, number of augmentations, backbone size, and pre-adaptation fine-tuning, which supports robustness of the design choices.
Complexity/efficiency analysis (FPS, trainable parameters) demonstrates the method's practicality relative to alternatives like TPT/VPT/DPE and full fine-tuning.
Reasonable theoretical grounding (cosine-Euclidean equivalence proposition) and qualitative visualizations connecting the mechanism (dense cluster weighting) to observed improvements.

Honest limitation discussion, e.g., IWE underperforming in scenes with many tiny, low-overlap objects (Cityscapes/BDD100K), and clear statement about why dataset-specific prompts were avoided despite giving larger gains.
weaknesses: Absolute gains are often modest, particularly for driving scenes (Cityscapes, BDD100K) and at high corruption severities on COCO-C, where the standard Adapter/TENT baseline sometimes matches or exceeds VLOD-TTA on specific corruptions, somewhat diluting the strength of the central claims.

IWE weighting proposals by connected-component size in an IoU graph is a relatively incremental technical contribution built on existing entropy minimization and NMS-adjacent ideas rather than a fundamentally new detection-adaptation paradigm.

No direct comparison to existing TTA-for-object-detection methods (e.g., Chen et al. 2023, Cao et al. 2025, Ruan & Tang 2024) even in an adapted/simplified form; the paper only compares to classification-style TTA baselines re-purposed for detection, leaving open how VLOD-TTA compares to detection-specific (non-VLM) TTA approaches.

Several hyperparameters (θ, γ, λ, ρ, M) show dataset-dependent optimal values (Fig. 6), and while the paper argues for a stable range, in a fully realistic online TTA setting without access to validation data this tuning is a practical limitation not fully addressed.

Reliance on GPT-generated prompt pools introduces a dependency on an external generative model whose exact output (and thus reproducibility) may vary across GPT versions/model updates; the prompt pool itself is not clearly frozen/released for exact reproducibility.

Results are reported without variance/confidence intervals across multiple runs or seeds, making it harder to assess the statistical robustness of the reported improvements, especially where margins over the Adapter baseline are small (e.g., driving scenes).
The abstract states 'Code:' with no actual link provided in the manuscript text, leaving reproducibility contingent on future release.

strengths: Addresses a clearly identified gap: TTA for vision-language object detectors, where only one prior specialized method (TTAOD-F) exists and it is costly (teacher-student, extra forward passes).

The two proposed components (IoU-weighted entropy minimization and image-conditioned prompt selection) are simple, well-motivated with clear qualitative illustrations (Figs. 1-2), and target specific, identifiable failure modes of naive entropy minimization and prompt averaging in the detection setting.

Extensive empirical validation across a wide range of shift types (style/texture, driving domains, low-light, 15 common corruptions on two datasets) and two structurally different VLODs (CNN-based YOLO-World and transformer-based Grounding DINO), totaling many test scenarios as claimed.

Thorough ablations: component-wise contribution (Table 3), adapter vs. batch-norm parameter choice, prompt averaging vs. selection, prompt-generation strategy, adapter placement, hyperparameter sensitivity (θ, γ, M, λ, ρ), batch size, augmentation count, and effect of pre-adaptation fine-tuning.

Direct efficiency and accuracy comparison with the only prior VLOD-TTA baseline (TTAOD-F), showing comparable or better accuracy with substantially fewer tuned/total parameters, lower memory, and lower latency.

Commendable transparency in reporting and analyzing a failure case (Cityscapes), diagnosing the causes (rider/person label overlap, small objects at low resolution) with a dedicated ablation rather than hiding the weaker result.

Additional generalization checks: backbone scaling (YW-L, GD-B) and a specialized domain (underwater Aquarium dataset), plus a theoretical note (cosine-Euclidean equivalence) motivating the compatibility score in IPS.
weaknesses: The adaptation is strictly single-image / single-step with parameters reset after each prediction, which is less a form of "online adaptation accumulating knowledge over a stream" and more a per-sample self-refinement; the practical benefit versus overhead trade-off in a true streaming/continual deployment scenario is not explored.

IWE's benefit is explicitly shown to degrade when proposal overlap is sparse (small objects, Cityscapes at low resolution), and the fix (higher input resolution) trades off inference cost/latency not fully quantified in the main comparison.

The TTAOD-F comparison is conducted only on COCO-C with Grounding DINO; a broader comparison (e.g., on the stylized/domain datasets or with YOLO-World) would strengthen the claim of consistent superiority over the sole prior method.

Some hyperparameters (γ, θ, ρ, λ, M) require per-architecture and somewhat dataset-sensitive tuning (e.g., different λ for YW vs GD), which could limit plug-and-play applicability despite the paper's efficiency claims; the sensitivity plots show non-trivial dataset dependence even if described as "stable."
Only two VLOD architectures (YOLO-World and Grounding DINO, plus their L/B variants) are evaluated; generalization to other open-vocabulary detector families is untested.

The main paper's efficiency comparison (Table 7) is reported only for YOLO-World; a similarly detailed cost comparison against all baselines for Grounding DINO would make the efficiency claims more complete.

Prompt pool generation relies on GPT-generated prompts (16 per class); reproducibility depends on this external, potentially non-deterministic prompt source, and sensitivity to prompt pool size/quality beyond the tested range is not deeply explored.

strengths: Addresses a relatively underexplored and timely problem: unsupervised test-time adaptation specifically for vision-language object detectors (VLODs), with only one prior specialized baseline (TTAOD-F) to compare against.

The two proposed components (IoU-weighted entropy, IWE; image-conditioned prompt selection, IPS) are intuitively motivated with clear qualitative illustrations (Figs. 1-2) that explain why naive entropy minimization and prompt averaging fail for detection.

Very extensive empirical evaluation: six domain-shift datasets, two corruption benchmarks (PASCAL-C, COCO-C) with 15 corruption types at 5 severities, two detector backbones (YOLO-World, Grounding DINO) and additional backbone variants (YW-L, GD-B), totaling a large number of test scenarios.

Thorough ablation studies: component contribution, adapter-vs-batchnorm, prompt generation/selection strategies, adapter placement per module, hyperparameter sensitivity (γ, θ, ρ, λ, M), batch size, augmentation count, and effect of pre-adaptation fine-tuning.

Honest and detailed failure-case analysis on Cityscapes (label overlap between 'rider'/'person' and small-object/low-resolution effects), which adds credibility and nuance rather than simply reporting favorable numbers.

Favorable efficiency profile relative to the only directly comparable specialized baseline (TTAOD-F): far fewer tuned/total parameters and substantially lower latency and GPU memory, while being roughly on par or slightly better in accuracy.
Additional generalization checks (specialized Aquarium underwater domain, different backbone sizes) support that the method is not narrowly overfit to the main benchmarks.
weaknesses: Accuracy gains over the most relevant and specialized prior method (TTAOD-F) are marginal and mixed rather than consistently superior (Table 5/16: overall mAP 26.2 vs 26.0 for the base model; TTAOD-F actually wins on several individual corruption types such as impulse noise, glass blur, contrast, elastic, pixelate, JPEG). The paper's main advantage over TTAOD-F is efficiency, but this is somewhat oversold as a general accuracy improvement in the abstract/conclusion.

On autonomous-driving scenes (Cityscapes, BDD100K) — arguably the most practically important real-world use case highlighted in the introduction — gains are small (+1.0 to +1.6 mAP) and the paper's own failure analysis shows IWE is fundamentally limited when proposal overlap is sparse (small objects), undermining claims of broad robustness.

Several design choices appear architecture-specific and somewhat ad hoc (different adapter insertion points for YOLO-World vs. Grounding DINO, different λ values, disabling head adapters for YW because fine-tuning the text encoder was found harmful), which complicates claims of a unified, architecture-agnostic framework and suggests nontrivial per-model engineering is needed in practice.

No reported variance/standard deviation across runs or multiple seeds; many reported gains (e.g., +0.3–0.6 mAP in several tables) are small enough that statistical significance is unclear, especially given single-adaptation-step, batch-size-1 evaluation.

The “theoretical justification” for IPS (Supp. 6.1) is a basic/trivial algebraic identity relating cosine similarity and squared Euclidean distance for unit-norm vectors, not a substantive theoretical contribution despite being framed as such.

Baselines adapted from classification TTA literature (TPT, VPT, DPE) to detection may not be optimally tuned for the detection setting, raising the possibility that some reported margins partly reflect weaker baseline implementations rather than a fundamentally stronger method.

Hyperparameter sensitivity analyses (Fig. 6) are conducted per-dataset and show non-trivial dataset dependence (e.g., optimal IoU threshold θ varies with object size), which is in tension with the paper's framing of TTA as a label-free, online setting where such per-domain tuning would not be available in deployment; it is not fully clear how robust the fixed default hyperparameters are to unseen domains not used in this tuning process.

Presentation is dense and the extracted figures/tables are sometimes hard to parse (e.g., small multi-panel sensitivity plots in Fig. 6-7, compressed text in Table 1), which may limit reproducibility and clarity without careful study of the supplementary material.

strengths: Addresses a genuinely underexplored and practically important problem—test-time adaptation for vision-language object detectors—and clearly differentiates itself from the only prior method (TTAOD-F), motivating the need for a lighter-weight, teacher-free alternative.

The two proposed components (IoU-weighted entropy minimization and image-conditioned prompt selection) are well motivated with clear illustrative examples (Figs. 1-2) that make the intuition (confirmation bias on isolated boxes, ineffectiveness of naive prompt averaging) easy to follow, and a short theoretical justification (cosine-Euclidean equivalence) is provided for the prompt-selection score.

Experimental evaluation is extensive: six domain-shift datasets, two corruption benchmarks (PASCAL-C, COCO-C, 15 corruption types x 5 severities), two structurally different detectors (CNN-based YOLO-World and transformer-based Grounding DINO), and additional backbone-scale and specialized-domain (Aquarium) experiments, lending good evidence of generality.

Direct comparison with the only prior VLOD-TTA method (TTAOD-F) shows comparable or better accuracy with substantially fewer tuned/total parameters and lower latency and memory, supporting the paper's efficiency claims.

Thorough ablations (component contribution, adapter vs. batch-norm, prompt averaging vs. selection, adapter placement, IoU-weighted pseudo-labeling as a generalizable principle) and an extensive hyperparameter sensitivity study in the supplementary material strengthen the technical soundness and reproducibility of the design choices.

The paper transparently investigates and explains its own failure case on Cityscapes (label overlap between 'rider'/'person' and small-object/low-resolution proposal sparsity), which is a mark of scientific honesty and adds useful insight rather than being hidden.
weaknesses: Despite claims of 'low additional overhead,' the method still requires per-image backpropagation at test time and is only marginally faster than the Adapter baseline (Table 7) and clearly slower than zero-shot inference, which somewhat tempers the 'low overhead' framing for real-time deployment.

Absolute gains are often modest on some benchmarks (e.g., ~+1.0 mAP on Cityscapes/BDD100K, ~+0.2-0.3 mAP average on COCO-C at some severities), and given TTA results are typically reported from single runs, the lack of variance/seed analysis makes it hard to judge whether gains are statistically robust versus noise.

The framework depends on several interacting hyperparameters (θ, γ, M for IWE; λ, ρ for IPS), and although the supplementary sensitivity analysis shows plausible stable ranges, the paper acknowledges elsewhere that per-dataset tuning (e.g., of batch-norm learning rates) is impractical in true TTA settings—raising the question of whether the chosen defaults truly transfer to unseen deployment domains without any access to held-out validation data.

IPS's benefit is partly entangled with the quality/richness of the GPT-generated prompt pool (16 prompts/class via ChatGPT-5), introducing an external, potentially non-reproducible dependency (prompt sets could vary with LLM version) that is not fully controlled for in the main comparison against baselines using simpler prompt schemes.

Comparison to alternative TTA-for-detection methods cited in related work (e.g., STFAR, contrastive alignment methods, fully test-time OD adaptation) is largely omitted beyond the custom Adapter/TPT/VPT/DPE baselines and TTAOD-F; a broader empirical comparison against these closed-set OD-TTA methods (adapted where feasible) would better substantiate the significance of the proposed gains.
